title: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
summary: Delegating object creation so callers stop depending on concrete classes — one product at a time with Factory Method, or a matched family at once with Abstract Factory.

slides.markdown: Both Factory Method and Abstract Factory exist to stop callers from writing `new ConcreteClass()` directly, so swapping implementations doesn't mean hunting down every call site. **Factory Method** lets a subclass decide which single class to instantiate; **Abstract Factory** hands out an entire *family* of related objects — like a UI kit's buttons and checkboxes — guaranteed to match. Think of Factory Method as one vending machine slot, and Abstract Factory as choosing which fully-stocked vending machine to use.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: new couples you to a concrete class
slides.markdown:
Calling `new MySqlConnection()` directly inside business logic hard-wires that logic to one concrete class — every place that needs a connection now has to know about MySQL specifically, and how to construct one correctly (host, port, pool settings).

This becomes a real cost the moment you need a second implementation: swapping in `PostgresConnection` for one environment means finding and editing every `new MySqlConnection()` call site, not just adding a class.

The fix in both Factory Method and Abstract Factory is the same shift: callers ask for "a connection" through an interface, and something else decides which concrete class actually gets built.

Takeaway: `new` is a coupling point — patterns in this topic move it somewhere you control centrally.

slides.sectionTitle: Factory Method: delegate construction to a subclass-overridable method

slides.markdown:
<<< Image: two parallel class hierarchies — DialogBox/WindowsDialogBox/MacDialogBox (creators) each paired via createButton() with Button/WindowsButton/MacButton (products) >>>

Factory Method always has two parallel hierarchies: a **creator** hierarchy (the class with the factory method) and a **product** hierarchy (what it returns). Each creator subclass pairs with exactly one product subclass.

The parallel-hierarchy shape is the tell — if you see two class trees where each subclass on one side always returns a matching subclass on the other, that's Factory Method.

slides.sectionTitle: Abstract Factory: a factory of related factories
Diagram: Abstract Factory producing a matched UI theme
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: DarkUiFactory and LightUiFactory each producing a matched pair — Button + Checkbox — with an X marking the mismatched cross-combination (DarkButton with LightCheckbox) as forbidden >>>

Swap `DarkUiFactory` for `LightUiFactory` at one injection point, and every button and checkbox created afterward switches themes together — there's no code path that can mix a dark button with a light checkbox, because both come from the same factory call.

That's the structural guarantee Abstract Factory buys you: consistency across a whole family, enforced by the type system rather than by convention.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory vs a plain constructor
slides.markdown:
Three ways to get an object, in increasing order of flexibility and complexity.

| | Produces | Extensibility | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain constructor | One concrete class, directly | None — every caller is coupled to it | Lowest |
| Factory Method | One product, chosen by a subclass | Add a new creator subclass per variant | Medium |
| Abstract Factory | A whole family of related products | Add a new factory implementation per family | Highest |

**How to decide:** start with a plain constructor. Move to Factory Method when one product needs to vary by subclass. Move to Abstract Factory only when *multiple* products must vary together as a set — reaching for it for a single product is over-engineering.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: swapping a concrete factory to retarget an entire product family
slides.markdown:
Abstract Factory's real payoff shows up at the single injection point where the factory is chosen.

```java
UiFactory factory = darkModeEnabled
    ? new DarkUiFactory()
    : new LightUiFactory();

Dialog dialog = new Dialog(factory);
dialog.render(); // every widget it creates matches the chosen theme
```

Everything downstream of `factory` — every button, checkbox, and menu the `Dialog` creates — retargets to the new family the moment this one line changes. No other code in the application needs to know dark mode exists.

That single point of change is the entire argument for Abstract Factory: without it, "switch to dark mode" would mean editing every `new LightButton()` call across the codebase.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for Abstract Factory when there's only ever one product family
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'm creating related objects, so I should use Abstract Factory to future-proof it."

**Why it's wrong:** Abstract Factory's entire value is letting you swap between *multiple* families. If your application will only ever have one UI theme, one database vendor, or one cloud provider, the interface and factory class are pure overhead — extra indirection with no swap to ever perform.

**Correct model:** introduce Abstract Factory when a second family is real or near-certain, not hypothetical. If you genuinely don't know whether a second family is coming, a plain constructor or a simple Factory Method is enough until the need is concrete — you can add the factory interface later without breaking callers, since they already go through one function.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up in real libraries: connection/driver factories
slides.markdown:
Factory patterns aren't academic — they're why `DriverManager.getConnection(url)` in JDBC works the way it does. The caller asks for "a connection" via a URL or config, and a factory underneath picks the concrete driver class matching the scheme (`jdbc:mysql:` vs `jdbc:postgresql:`).

This is exactly Factory Method at the scale of an entire ecosystem: every JDBC driver registers itself, and `DriverManager` decides which one to instantiate based on the connection string, so application code never names a concrete driver class.

Recognizing this pattern in a library you already use is often more convincing in an interview than reciting a UML diagram from memory.
